title: TEMPLATE: Style Guide (copy any element)
dek: Every element the site can make from Notion. Copy the block you need and paste it into your page.
html:
How to copy any element: hover the block below its gray line → click the ⋮⋮ handle on its left → Copy (or click the block and press Cmd+C) → go to your page → click an empty line → Cmd+V. Then change the words. The gray lines explain each block; do not copy them. See this page on the site at adjoakittoe.com/#template-styleguide.

Headings

The page title is the Title field of the row. Notion Heading 1 (/h1) starts a section like this one. The headings below are the smaller sizes. Copy the one you need.

This is Heading 4 on the site (Notion /h2)

This is Heading 5 on the site (Notion /h3)
This is Heading 6 on the site (Notion /h4)

Another way, typed on a normal line: start the line with h5: or h6: and a space.

This line becomes Heading 5
This line becomes Heading 6

Text

Select words, then use the toolbar. Highlight: A → Background → Yellow. Muted: A → Text → Gray. Tag: A → Background → Gray. Keyboard key: inline code on 1 to 3 characters. Hashtag: inline code that starts with #.

Body text with bold, italic, underline, struck, a highlight, muted words, a Tag, a key like ⌘ + K, a hashtag #recipe, and inline code.

A whole muted line: click the block ⋮⋮ → Color → Gray.

Muted text, for meta and supporting lines.

Hover text and hover photos

Hover text: select the word AND the words in brackets after it → A → Text → Blue. The brackets do not show on the site; their words pop up on hover.

Hover photo: color the word purple (A → Text → Purple). Put a photo anywhere on the page with the caption Hover: and the same words. Add | and a short caption if you want one. The photo itself stays hidden.

Working example of the Recipe template (same layout as Curried Fonio Pilaf). See it at adjoakittoe.com/#example-recipe. The section menu on the right is made from your Heading 1s. Side notes sit in the margin. To start your own: ••• (top right) → Duplicate → rename it, change the Slug, delete the gray lines and this box.

Headnote

Every Heading 1 becomes a section and a link in the side menu. Ingredients, Method, and Notes get their colors automatically.

A five-minute grain and a ten-minute pilaf. Onion and ginger do most of the work.1

a Side note in the margin. Make one: click at the end of the paragraph or step, press Enter, press Tab, type /callout. Side notes get letters a, b, c for you.

Ingredients

Heading 1 named exactly Ingredients, then bullets. Start each with an amount and a unit (cup, tbsp, tsp, g, oz, can, clove, small, pinch). The Serves buttons (from the Serves property) multiply the amounts. A line with no amount is left as is.

Serves
  • ½ cup fonio
  • 1 tbsp oil, for coating the fonio
  • 1 cup water
  • ½ tsp salt
  • 1 small onion, diced
  • Herbs and a lime, to finish

Method

Heading 1 named exactly Method, then a numbered list. Start each step with bold words.

  1. Cook the fonio. Coat the fonio with the oil, add the water and salt, cover, and cook on low about 5 minutes.1
  2. Build the base. Sauté the onion in a large pan for 3 to 5 minutes.
  3. Fold. Fold in the fonio and turn off the heat.

b Soggy? Cook off the remaining liquid. Dry? Add a spoonful of water.

To serve

Finish with herbs and a squeeze of lime.

Notes

Heading 1 named exactly Notes, then bullets.

  • Fonio is forgiving, so small changes in water are fine.
  • Make it a bowl with roasted vegetables.

Sources

  1. 1
    Yolélé Fonio, product packaging ↗ Brand
    Cooking time and yield, as printed on the bag.

title: TEMPLATE: The Pantry
dek: What to keep on hand when you’re getting started in the kitchen: the staples, a few favorites, and the tools that do most of the work.
sideLine: Start small. Buy what you’ll cook this month, then build.
html:
TEMPLATE (Guide). A copy of The Pantry built from Notion blocks. See it at adjoakittoe.com/#template-pantry. Sections with headings, lists, and tables are written below. The Other tools tiles and Where to start come from the Guide Items database (rows whose Page is this page). To make your own: ••• (top right) → Duplicate → change Title and Slug → delete this box → tick Publish.

The staples

Grains and starches

  • Brown rice and jasmine rice
  • fonio cooks in about five minutes
  • Quinoa
  • Rolled oats
  • Dried pasta
  • Spelt or all-purpose flour

Alkaline and plant-forward

  • Amaranth, teff, and wild rice
  • Sea moss
  • Hemp seeds
  • Walnuts and Brazil nuts
  • Dates
  • Key limes
  • Leafy greens like kale and callaloo

Beans and legumes

  • Chickpeas, dried or canned
  • Black beans
  • Black-eyed peas
  • Lentils red cook down soft; green and brown hold their shape

Oils and fats

  • Avocado oil or grapeseed oil for high heat
  • Extra virgin olive oil for low heat and finishing
  • Red palm oil, for West African dishes
  • Unrefined coconut oil
  • Butter or ghee

Acids

  • White vinegar a must, for cooking, pickling, and cleaning
  • Raw apple cider vinegar, with the mother
  • Rice vinegar
  • Lemons and limes

Salt and seasoning

  • Sea salt or kosher salt for cooking
  • Flaky salt for finishing
  • Whole black peppercorns and a grinder
  • Tamari or coconut aminos

Spices, whole

  • Cumin and coriander seeds
  • Grains of paradise
  • Grains of Selim
  • Cardamom pods
  • Cloves
  • Whole nutmeg
  • Allspice berries
  • Star anise
  • Bay leaves

Spices, ground and blends

  • Turmeric
  • Smoked paprika
  • Cayenne
  • Ground ginger
  • Cinnamon
  • Curry powder
  • Suya spice (yaji)
  • Berbere
  • Sumac
  • Dried thyme and oregano

Cans and jars

  • Whole peeled tomatoes
  • Tomato paste
  • Coconut milk
  • Low-sodium vegetable stock
  • Natural peanut butter just peanuts and salt, for groundnut soup
  • Dijon mustard

Sweet and baking

  • Raw honey
  • Blackstrap molasses
  • Maple syrup
  • Coconut sugar
  • Vanilla bean paste
  • Baking soda
  • Baking powder

On the counter and in the fridge

  • Onions
  • Garlic
  • Fresh ginger and turmeric root
  • Scotch bonnets or another hot pepper
  • Eggs

Storage and cleanup

  • Glass jars, for buying in bulk
  • Beeswax wraps
  • Unbleached parchment paper
  • Cotton or linen towels in place of paper
  • White vinegar and baking soda, for cleaning
  • A compost bin

Ground spices fade within a year or so. Buy small amounts, and buy whole when you can.

A few favorites

Kewpie

Japanese mayonnaise made with egg yolks and rice vinegar. Richer and tangier than American mayo.

Use it for dressings, sandwiches, roasted vegetables, and quick dips.

Black garlic

Whole garlic aged at low heat for weeks until the cloves turn black, soft, and sweet, with notes of balsamic and molasses.

Use it for mashing into butter, stirring into dressings and sauces, or spreading on toast.

Saffron honey

Honey infused with saffron threads. Floral, a little earthy, and golden.

Use it for yogurt, toast, roasted carrots, tea, or a honey vinaigrette.

Knives

KnifeWhat it’s for
Chef’s knife, 8 inchMost of your cutting: chopping, slicing, and dicing. The one worth spending on.
Paring knifeSmall work in your hand: peeling, trimming, and coring.
Serrated bread knifeAnything with a crust or a skin: bread, tomatoes, and cakes.
Santoku (optional)A Japanese all-purpose knife with a flatter edge, good for thin, even slices.
Boning knife (optional)Breaking down poultry and trimming meat.

Hone the edge often, sharpen it a few times a year, and wash knives by hand.

Pots and pans

PieceMaterialBest forCare
Skillet, 10 to 12 inchCast ironSearing, cornbread, and moving from stove to oven. Holds heat well.Dry it right away and wipe on a thin coat of oil. The seasoning builds as you cook.
Skillet, 10 to 12 inchStainless steelBrowning, pan sauces, and acidic foods like tomatoes.Heat the pan before adding oil to cut down on sticking. Safe to scrub.
SkilletCeramic nonstickEggs, pancakes, and delicate foods.Low to medium heat, and no metal utensils.
Dutch oven, 5 to 7 quartEnameled cast ironBraises, stews, soups, beans, and bread.Avoid heating it empty on high, and skip metal scrubbers on the enamel.
Saucepan, 2 to 3 quartStainless steelGrains, sauces, and reheating.Safe to scrub.
Stockpot, 8 quart or largerStainless steelStock, pasta, and big batches.Safe to scrub.
Sheet pansAluminumRoasting vegetables, sheet-pan dinners, and baking.Line with parchment for easy cleanup.

title: TEMPLATE: Fonio, A Small Grain With a Long Memory
dek: A tiny West African grain that cooks in five minutes, forgives your mistakes, and carries thousands of years of farming with it.
html:
TEMPLATE (Essay). A copy of the Fonio essay. See it at adjoakittoe.com/#template-fonio. Each Heading 1 is a section. 1 marks a citation; the matching source is item 1 under Sources at the end. Replace the sample photos with your own.

The relic

Fonio is easy to overlook. Each grain is tiny, and a bag of it looks more like sand than supper. But it has been prized across West Africa for more than 5,000 years1, and in Mali it is known as the seed of the universe, the grain at the root of all existence1.

This piece keeps it the way a reliquary keeps a relic: described, traced to where it comes from, and handled with care.

Catalog entry
ObjectFonio, a small grain
Also known asThe seed of the universe, in Mali
RegionWest Africa
Kept forMore than 5,000 years
Cooks inAbout five minutes
Yield1 cup dry makes about 4 cups cooked

Description

Fonio is an ancient grain1. Cooked, it turns light and fluffy, with a gentle nuttiness1. It is also gluten free2.

Provenance

Brands like Yolélé, co-founded by Senegalese chef Pierre Thiam, buy fonio from smallholder farming communities, with a mission to create economic opportunity for them3. Yolélé de-hulls its fonio using traditional methods in West Africa, so the odd bit of grit or husk is normal1.

Handling

Fonio cooks in about five minutes, and one cup of dry grain makes about four cups cooked1. People say fonio never embarrasses the cook1. Unlike rice, it forgives: if it comes out soggy, cook off the extra liquid; if it is dry, add a spoonful of water, cover, and give it a minute more1.

  1. One cup of dry fonio makes about four cups cooked.
  2. Coat the grains with oil before adding water.
  3. Fluff with a fork and serve.

Uses, catalogued

Sauté diced onion and ginger in olive oil for three to five minutes, then fold in cooked fonio and turn off the heat1. The full method is its own piece: Curried Fonio Pilaf →

One part fonio to four parts water or milk, with a pinch of salt1. It cooks into a soft, warm cereal in minutes.

Fonio also works in veggie burgers, in tabbouleh, as bread crumbs, and in gluten-free baking1.

What it holds

Fonio asks very little of the cook and gives back a lot. A grain kept and passed on for thousands of years is worth keeping well: described honestly, credited to the people who grow it, and cooked often.

For more, read my piece for the Institute of Culinary Education: Fonio Grain: A Legacy of Sustainability and Flavor↗.
